title: Masking & Its Cost
hook: Some people spend every conversation performing a face that is not theirs, and the better they are at it, the less anyone notices what it costs.
why:
Part II described the mask many men wear over distress: the cheerful I'm fine that hides strain. This chapter is about a deeper and more constant kind of mask. Many autistic people, and some people with ADHD and other differences, learn early that their natural way of moving, looking and speaking draws stares, teasing or rejection. So they learn to perform a different one, all day, every day.

Researchers call this camouflaging or masking. It can make someone seem perfectly at ease in a meeting or at a party. It can also leave them exhausted for days afterwards, unsure who they really are, and at risk of a collapse that others never saw coming, because the mask worked.

For a reader of people, masking is a humbling subject. It means that the smoothest, most socially fluent person in a room may be working harder than anyone, and that some of the signals you rely on have been deliberately produced to satisfy readers like you. This chapter covers what masking is, what it costs, why men do it too, how it relates to the masks everyone wears, what it can look like from outside, what happens when people stop, and how you can make it less necessary.

teach.p:
In 2017 Laura Hull, William Mandy and their colleagues asked 92 autistic adults to describe, in their own words, how they managed social life. Almost all described some form of what the researchers called camouflaging. It had two parts. Masking meant hiding natural behaviour: suppressing a stim, holding back an intense interest, forcing eye contact, keeping the face still or making it move as others' faces do. Compensation meant building strategies to get through: rehearsing conversations, copying the gestures and phrases of others, preparing jokes, studying how people react.

The reasons were understandable. People wanted to fit in, to make friends, to keep a job, and to avoid being bullied or singled out. Many had learned as children that their natural way of being was treated as a problem.

What makes masking hard to see is that, when it works, it looks like ordinary social skill. The person holds your gaze, nods at the right moments, smiles at the joke and asks a polite question about your weekend. Nothing in their body announces the effort.

For a reader, the lesson is that fluent social behaviour is not proof of ease. It may be the product of careful work, kept up because the person expects to be judged if it slips. The figure here stands composed, hands clasped in front, a picture of polite attention. You cannot tell from looking how much it costs him to hold.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic adults rarely described hiding their natural behaviour in social situations. Hull and colleagues found camouflaging described by almost all of the 92 adults they asked.

teach.p:
The adults in Hull's study described the consequences of camouflaging clearly. The first was exhaustion. Performing a different body all day takes attention and energy, and many described needing hours or days alone to recover from a single social event. Some described a loss of identity: after years of performing, they were no longer sure which parts of them were real.

In 2020 Dora Raymaker and her colleagues, working with autistic adults as research partners, described a state that many autistic people call autistic burnout. Its main features were chronic exhaustion, a loss of skills that had previously been manageable, such as speaking or organising daily life, and a reduced tolerance for noise, light and other stimulation. It arose when the demands placed on a person, including the demand to appear non-autistic, outstripped their capacity over a long period.

The researchers concluded that autistic burnout was distinct from ordinary job burnout and from depression, and that it could have serious effects on health and independence. Other research has linked heavy camouflaging with poorer mental health. Part II's chapters on burnout and depletion describe what can be noticed in anyone; here the point is that the cause may be invisible.

If you or someone you know is in this state and struggling to cope, the crisis resources in this app list where to turn. The figure here sits hunched and closed, the posture that may follow a day of performing, once no one is watching.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if camouflaging carried no cost for the people who did it. Autistic adults consistently describe exhaustion and loss of identity, and Raymaker and colleagues identified a distinct state of burnout linked to long-term demands to appear non-autistic.
teach.pullQuote: The smoothest person in the room may be working harder than anyone in it.

teach.p:
Much of the public discussion of masking has focused on autistic women and girls, and for good reason. In 2020 Hull and her colleagues surveyed more than three hundred autistic adults and found that, on average, autistic women reported more camouflaging than autistic men. Many women were diagnosed late, or not at all, partly because they masked so effectively.

But the same study found that autistic men camouflage too, and so do non-autistic people of all genders to some degree. Many autistic men, particularly older men, grew up before autism was widely recognised. They were simply told to toughen up, to look people in the eye, to stop being odd. Many learned to do so.

For men, masking also overlaps with the ordinary demands of masculinity that run through this book: do not show fear, do not cry, do not seem strange. An autistic man may be hiding both his autism and his distress about the effort of hiding it, behind the same calm face. A later chapter in this part looks at masculinity itself as a performance.

The practical point is not to assume that masking is something only other people do. The man in the next seat, or in the mirror, may be doing it. The figure here stands open and at ease, a posture that can be natural or can be held in place by effort. The body alone will not say which.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men did not camouflage at all. Hull and colleagues found autistic women reported more camouflaging on average, but autistic men reported it too.

teach.p:
It is worth placing autistic masking alongside the masks everyone wears. The chapter on the poker face earlier in this book described surface acting: showing an emotion you do not feel because a job requires it, such as smiling at a difficult customer. Alicia Grandey's research found that surface acting is tiring and linked to emotional exhaustion. Most people know the feeling of a long day of being pleasant.

A later chapter in this part looks at code-switching: changing how you speak, move and dress to fit a setting where your natural style is judged harshly. Many people from minority backgrounds describe it in terms very close to autistic masking.

What distinguishes autistic masking is its scope. A shop assistant surface-acts at work and goes home. Many autistic people mask in almost every social situation, including with friends and family, and some have done so since early childhood. The mask covers not just emotions but the basic mechanics of gaze, movement, voice and timing.

Seeing the continuity helps a reader in two ways. It makes autistic masking easier to understand from the inside, because you have done a small version of it yourself. And it makes clear that the burden is not inevitable: it grows or shrinks depending on how much the people around someone demand a performance. The figure here listens attentively, the kind of performed attention many jobs and many social situations require.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if surface acting and similar everyday masks carried no cost. Research on emotional labour links them to exhaustion, which makes the scale of autistic masking easier to grasp.

teach.h: What masking can look like from outside.
teach.p:
Masking is designed to be invisible, and you should not try to detect it. Speculating about whether someone is masking autism is a form of diagnosis, and it is not your business. But a few patterns, described by many people who mask, are worth knowing, because they change how you read someone you already know.

One is the gap between performance and recovery. Someone is warm and fluent at an event, then disappears for days, cancels plans or seems flat and withdrawn afterwards. Another is a sense of rehearsal: conversations that follow familiar scripts, jokes that seem prepared, questions asked in a set order. A third is a sharp difference between settings: relaxed and distinctive with one or two trusted people, smooth and conventional with everyone else.

None of these is a sign of autism. They are signs that social effort has a cost for this person, and that what you see in public is only part of the picture. The right response is not to probe but to reduce the demands you place on them.

It is also worth noticing your own part in it. If someone's natural manner has drawn comment from you, a raised eyebrow at a stim, a joke about a monotone, a request to look at you, you have taught them to mask in your company. The figure here walks slowly away, head down, the posture of someone leaving a social event with nothing left.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people who mask showed no difference between their public performance and their private recovery. People who mask consistently describe needing time alone afterwards, and Hull's participants named exhaustion as a central consequence.

teach.p:
In recent years many autistic people have written and spoken about unmasking: deliberately allowing themselves to stim, avoid eye contact, speak in their natural voice and follow their interests in front of others. Many describe it as a relief, and some describe their mental health improving as a result.

Unmasking also carries risks, and the choice belongs entirely to the person. Natural autistic behaviour still draws stares, jokes and judgments, and the first impressions research described in the previous chapter shows how quickly observers form negative views. Someone who unmasks at work may pay a price in how they are treated, even if they are better at their job for it.

This is why the question of masking is really a question about everyone else. The person who masks is responding to an environment. If the environment becomes more accepting, the mask becomes less necessary. That is something a reader of people can directly influence.

It also means that if someone unmasks with you, letting you see the stim, the averted gaze, the level voice, they are showing a kind of trust. Treat it that way. Do not comment on the change, and do not ask them to go back. The figure here sits wearing headphones, gaze lowered, an accommodation that many people only allow themselves where they feel safe.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if unmasking carried no social risk. The research on first impressions of autistic people shows that natural autistic behaviour is still often judged harshly, which is why the decision belongs to the person.

teach.p:
You cannot remove someone's mask, and you should not try. You can make it less necessary in your company.

Let movement be. Do not comment on fidgeting, rocking, pacing or fiddling with an object, and do not stare at it. Do not ask for eye contact or treat its absence as rudeness. Accept a level voice and a still face as normal for this person. Take words at face value, and say what you mean in return.

Reduce the load. Offer quieter places and smaller groups, side-by-side activities rather than face-to-face interrogation, agendas before meetings and time to answer. Accept no to social invitations without pressing, and offer lower-demand alternatives: a walk with one person rather than a party.

Avoid the well-meant comments that land badly. You don't seem autistic is usually meant kindly but tells the person that the mask is what you value. Everyone is a bit autistic dismisses the effort they make. If someone tells you they are autistic or have ADHD, the best response is usually simple: thank them for telling you, and ask whether there is anything that would make work or time together easier. The figures here walk side by side, the kind of low-pressure company in which many people can let the mask slip.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the behaviour of others made no difference to how much someone needed to mask. Autistic adults describe masking as a response to judgment and rejection, so reducing judgment should reduce the need.

poseGallery.annotation: Every comment on someone's natural movement teaches them to mask in your company. Let it be.

caseStudy:
Owen, forty-six, is a quantity surveyor known at work for being reliable, polite and a bit formal. He makes good eye contact, asks colleagues about their families and laughs at the right moments in meetings. At home, his wife has learned that after a work social he will spend the whole weekend almost silent, in the garden or with headphones on.

When their son was diagnosed as autistic at nine, Owen went with his wife to the assessment. As the psychologist described the boy's traits, Owen found himself recognising most of them in himself: the overwhelming noise of crowds, the effort of faces, the scripts he had written for small talk since secondary school. He was assessed himself the following year, and was told he was autistic.

The diagnosis did not change his behaviour at work overnight. But it changed how he understood his exhaustion. He stopped forcing himself to every social event and began taking a quiet lunch alone without guilt. He told his manager, who asked what would help. Owen asked for agendas before meetings and permission to keep his camera off on long video calls.

His manager agreed, and later admitted she had always thought Owen was the most socially confident person on the team. He told her, carefully, that he had been working very hard to seem that way, and that he would like to work a little less hard at it. She said that was fine, and that she was glad he had told her. It was the first time in twenty years at work that he had said it aloud.
observe: Notice someone this week who seems socially effortless, and consider how little you know about what it costs them.
Notice any comment you make, or hear, about someone's fidgeting, voice, gaze or manner, and what it teaches them.
Notice your own small masks: the pleasant face at work, the laugh at a joke you did not find funny, and how you feel afterwards.
Notice whether the people you know have places or company where they seem more themselves, and what those settings have in common.

drills.name: Mask Inventory
steps: List three situations this week where you performed a manner that was not natural to you.
For each, note what you hid or produced: a smile, a laugh, eye contact, a tone of voice.
Rate how tired you felt afterwards, from one to five.
Choose one situation where you could safely drop a little of the performance next time.

drills.name: No Comment Week
steps: For one week, make no comment on anyone's fidgeting, gaze, voice or way of sitting.
Each time you feel the urge, notice what you were about to say and why.
Write down how often it happened.
Reflect on what those comments might have taught the people on the receiving end.

drills.name: Offer a Lower-Demand Option
steps: Think of a friend or colleague who often declines group events or seems drained by them.
Offer them a lower-demand alternative: a walk, a coffee for two, a message instead of a call.
Make it easy to say no without explanation.
Notice how they respond, and what it tells you about what suits them.

drills.name: Better Responses
steps: Write down what you would say if someone told you they were autistic or had ADHD.
Check it against this chapter: does it thank them and ask what helps, or does it comment on how they seem?
Practise saying it aloud once, so it comes naturally when it matters.

quiz.q: A friend says that a colleague cannot be struggling socially, because he is always relaxed, chatty and makes great eye contact. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, because social fluency is a reliable sign that someone finds company easy
Fluent social behaviour may be the product of effort, and its cost may only show later
Great eye contact proves the colleague is not autistic, so he cannot be masking at all
Anyone who seems relaxed must be pretending, so the colleague is certainly struggling
quiz.explain: Masking is designed to look like ease. Many people who mask describe exhaustion and long recovery afterwards, so a smooth performance tells you little about the effort behind it.

quiz.q: Which consequences of camouflaging did the autistic adults in Hull and colleagues' 2017 study describe?
options: Exhaustion and threats to their sense of who they were
Greater energy, because fitting in made social life easier
No consequences, because the strategies became automatic
Better friendships, with no cost to their own well-being
quiz.explain: Participants described exhaustion and a loss of identity, alongside the benefits of fitting in. The effort of performing a different body all day does not disappear with practice.

quiz.q: What did Hull and colleagues' 2020 survey find about camouflaging and gender?
options: Only autistic women camouflaged; autistic men did not do it at all
Autistic men camouflaged more than autistic women on every measure
Autistic women reported more camouflaging on average, but men did it too
Non-autistic men camouflaged more than any other group in the survey
quiz.explain: On average autistic women reported more camouflaging than autistic men, but men camouflaged too. Many autistic men, especially older men, were never diagnosed and learned to mask without a name for it.

quiz.q: According to Raymaker and colleagues, which features characterise autistic burnout?
options: A short period of tiredness after a busy week, which a weekend's rest resolves
Anger at colleagues, together with a strong wish to leave a particular job
Low mood alone, which is identical to depression and treated in the same way
Chronic exhaustion, loss of skills and reduced tolerance of noise and light
quiz.explain: The researchers described chronic exhaustion, a loss of previously manageable skills and reduced tolerance for stimulation, arising when demands outstrip capacity over a long period. They found it distinct from job burnout and depression.

quiz.q: A colleague tells you he is autistic. You find yourself about to say that he does not seem autistic at all. What fits this chapter best?
options: Say it anyway, since it is meant as a compliment and he will take it that way
Thank him for telling you and ask whether anything would make work easier
Ask him to explain all his autistic traits, so that you can watch for them
Tell the rest of the team, so that they can adjust to him without asking
quiz.explain: You don't seem autistic tells him that the mask is what you value. Thanking him and asking what helps reduces the demand to perform, without probing or sharing what he told you in confidence.

quiz.q: A friend is lively and funny at every party, but you have noticed he usually cancels plans for several days afterwards. What is the most useful response?
options: Offer lower-demand ways to meet, like a walk for two, and accept no easily
Tell him he is being antisocial, so that he makes more of an effort next time
Stop inviting him to anything, since he clearly does not enjoy your company
Ask him directly whether he is autistic, so that you understand him better
quiz.explain: A gap between public performance and private recovery suggests that social effort is costly for him. Offering easier alternatives reduces the load without diagnosing or rejecting him.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific situation in which you hid your natural manner to fit in: at work, with family, at school, in a group of men. Describe what you suppressed or performed, how it felt at the time, and how you felt afterwards. Now think of someone in your life who may carry a heavier version of this. What is one thing you could stop doing, or start doing, that would make it easier for them to be themselves in your company?
reflection.guidance: You do not need to be autistic to have masked, and you do not need to know whether anyone else is. The aim is to understand the cost of performing from the inside, and to use that understanding to reduce the demands you place on others. Be specific about the setting and about the change you will make.

failureMode: The first failure is to read social fluency as proof of ease, when it may be the product of hard work. The second is to comment on someone's stim, gaze, voice or manner, teaching them to mask in your company. The third is to assume masking is something only autistic women do, when men, and everyone to some degree, do it too. The fourth is to try to detect or expose someone's mask, which is a form of diagnosis and not your business. The fifth is to treat recovery after social effort as rudeness. And the sixth is to say you don't seem autistic, as if the mask were the person.
